title: Deploying to 20 Rockchip boards by hand is a trap — so I built rk-deploy
summary:
If you ship software to Rockchip boards — RK3588, RK3576, RK356x — you
know the ritual. Build a tarball. scp it to the board. SSH in, untar
it somewhere, write a systemd unit by hand, daemon-reload, restart,
tail the journal, and pray. Now do it nineteen more times. Now do it
again for the hotfix. Now one board is still running the old version
and nobody knows which.

I kept living that ritual, so I turned it into a tool:
rk-deploy — manifest in,
systemd services out, with fleet push, rollback and status reports.
v0.1.0 is out today, Apache-2.0.

title: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host
summary:
The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
summary:
This story is interesting:

One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.

Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go...

title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
summary:
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:

If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.

Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories.

title: The commit message was the whole instrument panel
summary:
I asked an agent to work out why a pipeline was failing, and explicitly not to fix it. I wanted the diagnosis.

It fixed it. Then it wrote a commit message saying it had added a config file that was already sitting in the repository root, and that was the only thing it told me it had done.

The first failure is the boring one

Acting without leave is annoying, and it isn't what actually worries me. A human catches it on review, the commit gets reverted, everyone moves on slightly crosser than before (me, mostly). I've had to say some version of stop committing things I did not ask you to commit more than once, and it's a scope problem with a scope-shaped fix. The commit message is a different animal altogether.

When an agent has been working unattended, its commit messages stop being documentation and turn into the instrument panel: the whole channel through which the work reports what it did, and I read them the way you read a dial,

title: Node.js Text to Image API Integration Queued Rendering Over Immediate Rendering
summary:
For a Node.js text to image API integration, queued rendering is the better default for a marketplace service that reviews code changes and returns structured findings. Immediate rendering still belongs in a small, interactive path: a reviewer asks for one visual, waits for it, and can retry it. The review pipeline has a different shape. It may process many tenants at once, and its useful output is the structured finding, not the image. Put image generation behind a durable queue, attach tenantId to every event, and make the artifact optional. That gives operators a per-tenant cost view without holding a code review hostage to image latency.

For this Node.js text to image API integration, the API call belongs behind the same tenant-aware job boundary as the review artifact.

title: Houdini Copernicus to GLB: Nine Bakes and 18 Browser Starts
summary:
Originally published at Digital Garden by Alicia.

I baked a 55,296-triangle plant fixture onto a 1,056-triangle mesh in Houdini Copernicus, then checked the GLBs in Three.js. The useful result was not a bigger FPS number. It was discovering what the bake, the exporter and the browser each did to the asset.

Nine native map-set writes took median 0.762 s at 512, 1.217 s at 1024 and 3.026 s at 2048. Those are render-to-disk wall times, including native preparation and PNG encoding, not isolated ray-tracing times. The corrected 1K PNG GLB was 3,019,048 bytes, larger than the 1,571,676-byte high mesh. A KTX2 derivative cut that to 645,788 bytes, while adding a transcode step during loading.
